2.text: Two other cases that I met personally were very young men living

3.text: with their parents. One was a nimble young fellow and a very able herdsman;

4.text: but the people accused him of perverting all his young companions, who

5.text: beset him with their courtship, to the great detriment and offence of the

6.text: lawful beauties of the camp. The other one was a sickly fellow, who,

7.text: however, was told to look seriously for a husband. Both were so “bashful” that

8.text: they carefully avoided giving me time or opportunity for any annoying questions.

9.text: I heard, also, of another “soft man,” who was woman-like in face, talked

10.text: in a thin, piping voice, and had very long hair. He changed his sex completely

11.text: from the very beginning of his “shamanistic” call.

12.text: The perversion of the sexual functions, resulting from psychical or

13.text: physical causes, may happen, of course, among primitive peoples as well as

14.text: among civilized ones. I met among the Russian creoles of the Lower Kolyma,

15.text: who do not differ practically from the Russianized Yukaghir of the same

16.text: locality, an old man who had a bearded face and the outer genital organs

17.text: of a male. Notwithstanding this, he acted like a woman throughout his whole

18.text: life. He wore woman’s dress, performed woman’s work, and even in his

19.text: conversation applied to himself the feminine gender, for which the Russian

20.text: language presents numerous occasions. The neighbors called him Supan,

21.text: (Жупанъ Супанъ), which is a local Russian term for a man of transformed

22.text: sex, and is likewise applied to native cases.¹

23.text: The case of qaˊčɪkɪčhêča, that is, of a woman transformed into a man,

24.text: is still more remarkable than that of the “soft man.” I obtained detailed

25.text: information of only two or three instances. One was of a widow of middle

26.text: age, who had three half-grown children of her own. She received at first an

27.text: “inspiration” of a more usual kind, but later the “spirits” wanted to change

28.text: her to a man. Then she cut her hair, donned the dress of a male, adopted

29.text: the pronunciation of men, and even learned in a very short time to handle

30.text: the spear and to shoot with a rifle. At last she wanted to marry, and

31.text: easily found a quite young girl who consented to become her wife.

32.text: The transformed one provided herself with a gastrocnemius from the leg

33.text: of a reindeer, fastened to a broad leather belt, and used it in the way of

34.text: masculine private parts. I have said before that the gastrocnemius of a

35.text: reindeer is used by Chukchee women for the well-known unnatural vice.

36.text: After some time the transformed husband, desiring to have children by her

37.text: young wife, entered into a bond of mutual marriage with a young neighbor,

38.text: and in three years two sons were really born in her family. According to

39.text: the Chukchee interpretation of mutual marriage, they were considered her own

40.text: lawful children. Thus this person could have had in her youth children of

41.text: ¹ The term “supan” is derived, probably, from the Kamchadal word “shopoˊnach,” which signified the

42.text: entrance-door of the Kamchadal winter hut. This entrance was tabooed to men, and only women and transformed

43.text: men were allowed to pass through it, while the men always used the roof-entrance (see Steller, p. 35, footnote).
